Solve the following problem step by step. Put your answer inside \boxed{}.

During a custodial interrogation, if a suspect is informed of the right to speak with an attorney before questioning but is not advised of the right to have counsel present during the interrogation, and subsequently makes incriminating statements without requesting a lawyer, should those statements be suppressed? Explain the legal basis for the court's ruling.
Remember to put your answer inside \boxed{}.

expected_answer: The statements are inadmissible because the suspect was not advised of his right to have counsel present during questioning. Under Miranda v. Arizona, the warnings must include the right to have an attorney present both before and during questioning to fully protect the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. Omitting the right to counsel during interrogation renders the warnings constitutionally inadequate, and any resulting statements are therefore inadmissible, regardless of whether the suspect requested an attorney or was coerced.
